name: FS KKR Capital Corp.

profile.description: FS KKR Capital Corp. is an externally managed business development company (BDC) advised by FS/KKR Advisor, a partnership of FS Investments and KKR Credit, lending to private US middle-market companies. Q2 2026 net investment income was $0.44/share (9.6% annualized on NAV), but NAV fell 2.8% to $18.30 after a $2.00/share markdown in Q1, and software exposure of 16.4% of the portfolio (including Medallia) has drawn AI-disruption concern. KKR committed a $150M tender and a $150M convertible preferred investment, the adviser waived incentive fees, and the quarterly distribution was reset to $0.42-0.44. Fitch downgraded FSK to junk, and a securities class action (Stuart v. FS KKR, E.D. Pa.) is pending.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (0/3): FSK remains a leveraged middle-market lending vehicle; its major change was the 2021 merger with FSKR, which added scale rather than a new business [4]. AI Deployment (0/2): Management has run AI risk assessments across portfolio holdings [5], but there are no AI products or quantified AI savings. Market Share (1/2): FSK is one of the largest public BDCs, sourcing through KKR's private credit platform [5], but direct lending is competitive and undifferentiated. Pipeline (0/2): There is no product pipeline; management guides only to NII of 8-9% of NAV for the rest of 2026 [1]. R&D Intensity (0/1): No R&D spending [4].

inspiration.label: WEAK
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (1/4): FSK's stated purpose of providing customized credit solutions to middle-market companies is generic for a BDC [7]. Community Impact (0/2): No distinctive charitable or community program was found for this externally managed vehicle. Employee Retention (0/2): FSK has no direct employees; it is run by its external adviser, and no retention data are available [7]. Insider Buying (0/2): KKR's $150M tender and $150M convertible preferred investment are sponsor capital support rather than open-market insider buying, and no meaningful executive purchases were found [2].

infrastructure.label: DEVELOPING
infrastructure.analysis: Calculated mechanically on the Dividend weighting (raw 4.04/10). Strengths are a 7.3 forward P/E, 13 consecutive years of distributions in the yfinance history (2014-2026), and a 23.8% 5-year investment-income CAGR (FMP interest income of $510M in 2020 to $1.48B in 2025, derived by us and inflated by the 2021 FSKR merger) [3][4]. ROE of -6.6%, a -28.5% profit margin, and a -27.1% revenue decline all score zero, and D/E of 123% scores 0.77 [3]. The distribution absorbs about 95.5% of NII (Q2 2026 distribution of $0.42 vs. NII of $0.44, derived), it has not grown, and trailing-12-month distributions of $2.04 vs. $2.45 five years earlier give a -3.6% 5-year CAGR (derived from yfinance history), which zeroes the double-weighted growth metric [1][3].

ai_resilience.label: HIGH RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (4/9): FSK is not itself displaced by AI, but its loan book is exposed: software and services are the largest sector at 16.4% of the portfolio, problem credits include software company Medallia, and management has had to run AI risk assessments across holdings [5]. CNBC reported that a JPMorgan-led bank group reduced credit to FSK amid portfolio stress tied in part to software exposure [2]. AI Opportunity (0/1): FSK earns no AI-related revenue.

infinite_game.summary: Through Sinek's lens, FSK plays a finite game: an externally managed yield vehicle whose purpose is producing a distribution, which it has now had to cut as credit losses mounted. The KKR capital support is a meaningful act, but it defends the franchise rather than advancing a cause.

just_cause.analysis: FSK's purpose is to generate income for shareholders from middle-market loans; there is no vision of a better future beyond yield [7]. A securities class action alleges management overstated portfolio restructuring and the durability of the distribution [6].

trusting_teams.analysis: FSK has no employees of its own and relies on an external adviser paid partly on incentive fees [7]. NAV losses of 46% in share value over a year, a Fitch downgrade to junk, and litigation point to an unstable situation, not a high-trust one [5][6].

worthy_rivals.analysis: No evidence was found of FSK treating other BDCs or private credit funds as benchmarks to learn from. Its communication focuses on its own credit cleanup [1].

existential_flexibility.analysis: FSK remains a leveraged middle-market lender; its response to stress has been asset sales, a smaller portfolio, and a distribution reset rather than any strategic reinvention [1].

courage_to_lead.analysis: The adviser waived incentive fees (adding $11M to Q2 NII), and KKR committed $300M of new capital through a tender and convertible preferred, real costs borne to stabilize the vehicle [1][2]. Earlier delays in addressing non-accruals, alleged in litigation, weigh against this [6].

investment_thesis: FSK trades at about 0.6x its $18.30 June 30 NAV and 7.3x forward earnings, with a roughly 16% yield, and KKR's $300M capital support plus fee waivers show the sponsor is defending the vehicle [1][2][3]. If non-accruals keep falling and NII holds at 8-9% of NAV, the discount could narrow [1].
thesis_continued: Credit quality is the problem: Q1 2026 brought a $2.00/share markdown, NAV fell again in Q2, total investment income is shrinking with the portfolio, and 16.4% software exposure faces AI disruption [1][5]. With a junk rating, a pending class action, and minimal Innovation, Inspiration, and Infinite Game scores, the IOWN score is SELL.
key_catalysts: Q3 2026 results showing whether non-accruals and NAV markdowns stabilize [1]
Completion of KKR's $150M tender and $150M convertible preferred investment [2]
$300M share buyback authorization at a deep discount to NAV [1]
key_risks: Further credit losses in software and healthcare borrowers such as Medallia and Affordable Care [5]
Junk credit ratings and bank lenders reducing exposure, raising funding costs [2][5]
Securities class action over valuation and distribution disclosures (Stuart v. FS KKR Capital Corp., No. 26-cv-02969) [6]
